tool_name: Rally (formerly CA Agile Central / Rally Software), by Broadcom — part of the ValueOps suite
target_user: Admin/IT-led. Initial setup requires a Subscription Administrator; Workspace Administrators are then delegated per workspace. Project Administrators can create child projects within their scope. Team-level configuration (boards, iterations, dashboards) is self-service for team members once the hierarchy is in place, but the foundational structure is explicitly not self-service.
setup_time_estimate: Days to weeks for a single ART; weeks to months for an enterprise SAFe rollout. Broadcom and partners (Rego, Winmill, ICON Agility) sell formal 'QuickStart' / 'Ready > Sync > Go' engagements to prepare a delivery group for their first Program Increment. Reviewers on G2 and Gartner Peer Insights repeatedly cite a 'steep learning curve' and recommend 'detailed training' before users are productive. Sources do not publish a concrete time-to-first-board figure — flagged uncertain.
onboarding_wizard: [uncertain] No modern in-product setup wizard surfaced in research. Rally provides a 'Learn Rally in Five Easy Steps' tutorial and a web-based training catalogue rather than a guided first-run flow. The mental model is: subscription admin creates the workspace, customises schedule/state/portfolio item names, then creates the project hierarchy (ART/team) and configures iterations and releases. There is no branching 'choose Scrum/Kanban/SAFe' wizard; SAFe is implemented by convention via the project hierarchy and portfolio item types.
template_library: [uncertain] Rally has a strong portfolio-item type system (Epic, Capability, Feature, Story by default, customisable per workspace) and a library of pre-built apps/panels for boards and dashboards. However, it does not appear to ship a modern, gallery-style 'template marketplace' equivalent to monday.com or Jira templates. Partner-provided SAFe configuration packs (Rego, Winmill) effectively serve as templates and are typically delivered as consulting artefacts rather than self-serve assets — hence flagged uncertain.
ai_assisted_setup: [uncertain] Public research surfaces no Rally-native AI setup assistant comparable to monday Sidekick or Atlassian Intelligence. Broadcom has been adding AI capabilities across ValueOps (ValueOps Insights, AI for analytics) but no documented 'AI configures my ART' feature was found in 2026 sources. Flagged uncertain pending vendor briefing.
hierarchy_config: Fixed-shape but customisable labels. The Rally model is: Subscription → Workspace → Project (hierarchical, used to represent ARTs / Solution Trains / teams) plus Portfolio Items (Epic → Capability → Feature) and team-level work (Story, Defect, Task). Releases represent Program Increments. Portfolio item names, schedule states, and workflow states are customisable per workspace. Setting the hierarchy up correctly is non-trivial and is the single biggest source of setup friction — getting ART/team project structure wrong forces painful re-parenting later. Rollups and reports are workspace-scoped, so Broadcom strongly recommends limiting the number of workspaces.
multi_team_setup: Designed for enterprise scale from day one — but admin-required at every level. ARTs are modelled as parent projects with team projects nested beneath; Solution Trains add another parent layer. Subscription admins create workspaces; only subscription/workspace admins can create top-level projects. A 10-team ART requires deliberate project hierarchy design and is typically a consulting engagement. Strengths: rollups, dependency views, capacity plans, and portfolio kanban work natively at the ART/Solution Train level — this is what Rally is built for.
admin_dependency: High. Three admin tiers (Subscription, Workspace, Project) gate most configuration: workspace creation, portfolio item type customisation, schedule states, work rules, connectors, and SSO are all admin tasks. Team members can create iterations within their project, manage their team board, build custom dashboards/apps, and edit work items, but they cannot reshape the hierarchy. The self-service vs admin boundary is clearly defined but skewed heavily toward admin.
permissions_model: Role-based and project-scoped. Roles: Subscription Admin, Workspace Admin, Project Admin, Editor, Viewer. Permissions cascade down the project hierarchy. Work Rules let workspace admins enforce field-level constraints. Praised as robust and auditable; criticised as 'complex' and a frequent source of new-user confusion. Reviewers on G2 note the UI exposes feature richness in ways that can overwhelm before permissions clarify what each user should see.
import_capabilities: Limited self-service. Rally can export to CSV/XML via the per-page Actions menu; CSV is the recommended export format. Import into Rally is typically done via the Web Services API, CA Agile Central Connector for Excel/Word, or partner ETL tooling — not a polished in-product CSV mapping wizard. The Atlassian Jira documentation maintains a Rally → Jira import path (one-way out of Rally), which is the more commonly documented migration direction. Bringing data into Rally cleanly almost always involves a partner.
migration_story: Real-world reports describe Rally migrations as significant projects. SPK and Associates publishes a 'Navigating Your Migration from Rally to Jira Without Losing Sanity' guide that is widely referenced. Third-party tools (cPrime Labs Rally-to-Jira Enterprise Migration Tool, Getint, Tasktop/Planview Hub) are commonly used. Basic CSV import preserves only titles/descriptions and loses attachments, comments, test artefacts, and relationships. Most enterprise migrations engage Broadcom partners (Rego, Winmill, ICON Agility) for either inbound or outbound moves.
vcs_integration_setup: Admin-led, connector-based. The Rally VCS Connector for GitHub / GitHub Enterprise is a separate component installed on a server (Python 3.5/3.6) and configured via a YAML policy file. It is one-way (Git → Rally), one-time per commit, and posts changeset data back to Rally artefacts. A newer 'Rally Bot' GitHub App provides a lighter integration. Connectors exist for Git, TFS/VSTS, Bitbucket, and Subversion. Time to first linked commit is hours-to-days depending on whether the connector host already exists and who owns GitHub Enterprise admin rights — this is not a 'click two buttons' integration.
slack_notifications_setup: Two-tier model. Notification preferences are configured per user in Rally Settings → Connected Accounts → Connect Slack, and notifications arrive as DMs from the RallyBot Slack app (no shared-channel spam). This is self-service per user. There is also a Slack plug-in for Broadcom Continuous Delivery Director, and community-built Rally→Slack integrations (e.g. bradrich/slack-rally on GitHub) for channel-level routing. Centrally-administered, board-level Slack notifications akin to monday.com automations are not surfaced in the same way.
first_impression_ux: Functional and dense rather than welcoming. Reviewers describe the UI as 'feature-rich', 'cluttered', and 'overwhelming for new users'. Day-one experience for a newly-provisioned user typically lands them on the Team Board / Track view of their assigned project, which is empty until iterations and stories are created. There is no auto-installed sample data or sample sprint. Broadcom's published 'Learn Rally in Five Easy Steps' tutorial is the closest the product comes to guided onboarding.
time_to_value: Slow. Rally rewards investment: once the ART hierarchy, portfolio item types, and PI cadence are configured, the platform delivers strong ART-level visibility (capacity plans, dependency board, portfolio kanban, PI roll-ups) that other tools struggle to match. But there is no free trial that lets a team self-discover this value — Broadcom moved to a no-cost / free Rally model for some segments in recent years, yet getting to the 'aha' moment still typically requires partner-led setup.
setup_complaints: Most common complaints from G2/Gartner/Peerspot: (1) 'Steep learning curve' for new users without training; (2) UI is 'cluttered' / 'overwhelming' / feature-rich in ways that confuse rather than guide; (3) Integrations setup is 'challenging' and connector-heavy; (4) Hierarchy mistakes are costly to undo; (5) Requires partner services for serious rollouts; (6) Limited modern AI/automation surface compared to monday/Jira/Atlassian; (7) Documentation is comprehensive but scattered across techdocs subtrees.
setup_praise: Most common praise: (1) Once configured, Rally is genuinely built for SAFe — ART, Solution Train, PI, Capability, Feature are first-class concepts not bolted on; (2) Robust roll-ups and reporting across the full portfolio hierarchy; (3) Capacity planning and dependency board are best-in-class for PI Planning; (4) Granular permissions and work rules suit regulated enterprises; (5) Extensive free web-based training catalogue; (6) Stable, mature, and deeply documented; (7) Mindshare among large SAFe shops remains high (Gartner: 6.5% EAP mindshare).
standout_setup_feature: First-class SAFe hierarchy. Rally is one of the very few tools where Agile Release Train, Solution Train, Program Increment, Epic, Capability, and Feature are real, native objects with native rollups — not custom fields layered on top of a generic issue tracker. For organisations fully committed to SAFe, this removes a class of modelling problems other tools force you to solve. The Capacity Plan view for PI Planning is the differentiating moment and is what keeps Rally in enterprise SAFe shortlists.
servicenow_comparison: Per PeerSpot and Gartner Peer Insights 2026, Rally and ServiceNow SPM/EAP compete in the same Gartner Magic Quadrant category. Rally is positioned as the 'deep SAFe purist' option with strongest team/ART-level agile depth; ServiceNow EAP is positioned as the platform play with strongest integration to ITSM, financials, and the broader ServiceNow Now Platform. Gartner Peer Insights 2026 ranks ServiceNow #5 (7.8) and Broadcom Rally #7 (7.2) in EAP; Rally holds 6.5% mindshare vs ServiceNow's 5.9%. Setup-wise both are admin-led and require partner engagement at scale, with ServiceNow's advantage being unified onboarding with other ServiceNow products an organisation already runs, and Rally's advantage being the maturity of its out-of-the-box SAFe object model.
